cueCard.title: Describe a colleague you enjoy working with.
points: how long you have worked together
what you usually do together at work
cueCard.final: and explain why you enjoy working with this person.

sample:
I'd like to talk about Fang, a designer on my team who I've worked with for nearly three years. She joined the company just a few months before me, so in my first weeks she was the person I kept going to with questions, and we've been a kind of informal partnership ever since.

Most of our work together involves putting marketing campaigns together. I usually come up with the overall idea and write the text, and she turns it into posters, short videos and social media graphics. We sit next to each other, so a lot of our best ideas come from quick chats across the desk rather than formal meetings. When we're under pressure, we also have a habit of going downstairs for a ten-minute walk to talk things through, which almost always helps.

There are a few reasons why I enjoy working with her so much. First of all, she's incredibly reliable. If she says something will be ready by Thursday, it's usually ready by Wednesday afternoon. She's also very direct, in a good way. If she thinks one of my ideas is weak, she'll tell me straight away, but she always explains why and suggests something better. At first I found that a bit uncomfortable, but now I really value it, because it saves us a lot of wasted effort.

On top of that, she has a great sense of humour. Even on the most stressful days, she can make the whole team laugh, which makes long evenings at the office much more bearable. If she ever moved to another company, work wouldn't be half as much fun.

part3.q: What makes a good colleague?
part3.sample: Reliability is probably the most important quality. In a team, everyone depends on each other, so one person who misses deadlines can hold up a whole project. Good communication matters too, especially being able to disagree politely without making things personal. Beyond that, a good colleague is willing to share knowledge rather than keeping it to themselves to look more valuable. Unfortunately, in very competitive workplaces, people are sometimes discouraged from doing that.

part3.q: Is it a good idea to become close friends with colleagues?
part3.sample: It has both advantages and risks. Having friends at work makes the day more enjoyable, and people who trust each other usually cooperate better. On the other hand, friendship can complicate things, for example if one friend is promoted and becomes the other's manager, or if there's a serious disagreement over a project. So it's fine to be friendly with everyone, but it's wise to be a little careful about mixing your private life and your career too much.

part3.q: How has working from home changed relationships between colleagues?
part3.sample: It's made relationships more task-focused. When everyone is in the same office, you chat by the coffee machine or have lunch together, and those small moments build trust. Online, most conversations are scheduled and stick to the agenda, so it's harder to get to know people as individuals. New employees are probably affected most, because they miss out on learning from experienced colleagues informally. That's partly why many companies now ask staff to come in on certain days.

part3.q: Do you think teamwork will become more or less important in the future?
part3.sample: I expect it to become more important. Many of today's problems, like developing new medicines or tackling climate change, are far too complex for any one person to solve. Even in ordinary companies, projects increasingly need people with different skills, such as designers, engineers and data analysts, to work closely together. Artificial intelligence might take over some individual tasks, but the ability to cooperate, negotiate and build on other people's ideas is likely to become even more valuable.

cueCard.title: Describe someone you know who is a good parent.
points: how you know him or her
what he or she does with his or her children
cueCard.final: and explain why you think this person is a good parent.

sample:
The person I'd like to describe is my friend Hao, who I met at university. We were both in the hiking club, and he was the first person among my close friends to get married and have a child. His daughter, Duoduo, is five now, and I see them every couple of months, usually when a group of us meets up for a weekend lunch.

What strikes me about Hao is how involved he is in his daughter's life. A lot of fathers I know leave most of the parenting to their wives or to the grandparents, but Hao does the school run every morning and reads to her every night, even when he's exhausted from work. At weekends, they go on what he calls little adventures, like visiting the wetland park to look for birds or cooking a simple dish together. Last time I visited, she proudly showed me a plate of scrambled eggs she'd made all by herself.

I think he's a good parent for a few reasons. First, he's patient. When she gets upset, he doesn't shout. He crouches down to her level and asks her what's wrong. Second, he takes her questions seriously. If she asks why the sky is blue, he doesn't brush her off. Instead, they look it up together. And finally, he isn't obsessed with making her the best at everything. Plenty of parents in our city sign their children up for five or six classes, but he lets her choose one activity she really enjoys and leaves the rest of her time free for play.

Watching him has definitely changed my idea of what good parenting looks like.

part3.q: What qualities does a good parent need?
part3.sample: Patience is near the top of the list, because children test your limits every single day. Good parents also need to be consistent, so that children understand the rules and the consequences of breaking them. I'd add the ability to listen. Many parents are so busy giving instructions that they never really find out what their child is thinking or worried about. Finally, a good parent sets an example, since children copy what adults do far more than what they say.

part3.q: Is it harder to be a parent today than it was in the past?
part3.sample: In some ways, yes. Previous generations had less money, but their expectations were simpler. As long as children were fed and went to school, parents felt they'd done their job. Today, parents worry about education, screen time and mental health, as well as competition from a very young age. Social media adds pressure, because people constantly compare their children with others. On the other hand, modern parents have far more information and support available, so it isn't harder in every respect.

part3.q: What role do grandparents play in raising children in your country?
part3.sample: A huge role. Because in many couples both partners work full-time, grandparents often look after young children during the day, and some even move to another city to help. This saves families a lot of money on childcare, and children grow up close to their grandparents. The downside is that the two generations don't always agree. Grandparents may be more relaxed about sweets or more traditional about discipline, which can lead to tension at home.

part3.q: Should governments offer parenting classes to new parents?
part3.sample: It would be helpful, as long as the classes are optional. Most of us receive years of training for our jobs but none for raising children, which is arguably far more important. Classes could cover practical things like child safety and nutrition, as well as how to handle tantrums calmly. They might also reduce stress for young parents who live far from their families. However, it would be wrong to force people to attend or to suggest there's only one correct way to bring up a child.

cueCard.title: Describe a young person you know who is very talented.
points: what he or she is talented at
how you found out about this talent
cueCard.final: and explain how you feel about this person's talent.

sample:
I'd like to talk about my younger cousin Xiaoyu, who's fifteen and still at secondary school. He's quite a quiet boy, the kind who disappears into a corner at family gatherings, but he has an amazing talent for drawing.

I found out about it by accident about two years ago. We were at my aunt's flat for the Mid-Autumn Festival, and while the adults were chatting, I noticed him sketching in a notebook. I asked if I could have a look, expecting a few doodles, but every page was full of detailed comic strips. He'd invented his own characters, a group of stray cats living in an old neighbourhood, and the drawings were packed with tiny details, like washing hanging from balconies and broken bicycles leaning against walls. One page showed a rainy street at night, and it looked almost like a photograph.

What impresses me most is that he's almost entirely self-taught. His school only has one art class a week, and his parents were quite worried at first that drawing would distract him from his studies. So he learned mainly by copying artists he admires and watching free tutorials online, often late at night after finishing his homework.

As for how I feel, it's a mixture of admiration and a little envy. I can't draw a straight line, and I never had that kind of passion for anything at his age. But mostly I'm just proud of him. I've been encouraging him to share his work, and last month he finally entered one of his comics in a competition for young artists. Whatever the result, I think he has a real future in illustration.

part3.q: Are people born with talents, or do they develop them through practice?
part3.sample: It's a combination of both. Some people clearly have a natural advantage, like a good ear for music or unusual physical coordination. But without years of practice, that advantage doesn't go very far. In fact, I've seen plenty of people with average ability overtake more gifted classmates simply because they worked harder and didn't give up. So natural talent might decide where you start, but effort largely decides how far you get.

part3.q: Should talented children be sent to special schools?
part3.sample: It depends on the child and the type of talent. For sports or music, specialist schools can provide coaching and facilities that an ordinary school can't offer. However, there's a risk of putting too much pressure on children at a very young age and narrowing their education too early. A child who spends all day practising the piano might miss out on friendships and other interests. Personally, I think extra classes alongside a normal school often strike a better balance.

part3.q: How can society help young people develop their talents?
part3.sample: Access is the key issue. Talented children from poorer families or rural areas often never get the chance to discover what they're good at, because lessons and equipment cost money. Governments could fund free after-school programmes and community centres, and offer scholarships to promising students. Companies and universities could run competitions and mentoring schemes as well. The internet has already helped a lot, but young people still need guidance and encouragement from real people.

part3.q: Will the talents that society values change in the future?
part3.sample: Almost certainly. A few decades ago, being able to do quick mental arithmetic or memorise large amounts of information was highly valued. Now computers do those things instantly, and with artificial intelligence improving so fast, even skills like translation are becoming less special. Talents that are distinctly human, such as creativity, empathy and leadership, are likely to be valued more. The ability to learn new skills quickly could also become a talent in itself, because jobs are changing so rapidly.

cueCard.title: Describe a place in the countryside that you visited.
points: when and why you went there
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about this place.

sample:
I'm going to talk about a small village in the hills about two hours' drive from my city. I went there last April on a team-building trip organised by my company. Our manager wanted us to get away from screens for a weekend, so she booked a guesthouse run by a local family, and twelve of us set off on a Friday afternoon in a rented minibus.

The village itself is quite small, with maybe a hundred households. Most of the houses are built of grey stone, and they're spread out along a stream that runs down from a bamboo forest. Because a lot of the young people have moved to cities for work, the village is very quiet, and most of the residents we met were in their sixties or seventies.

We packed a lot into two days. On Saturday morning, the guesthouse owner took us up into the forest to dig for bamboo shoots, which was much harder work than it looked. In the afternoon, we helped his wife make dumplings, and we were all hopeless at folding them. In the evening, we sat in the courtyard eating the food we'd prepared, and because there was so little light pollution, we could see more stars than I'd ever seen in my life.

I felt incredibly relaxed there, almost as if time had slowed down. It also made me a bit sad, though. The owner told us that the village school had closed years earlier because there weren't enough children left. It made me realise how fast rural life is changing, and I came home wanting to visit places like that more often, before they disappear.

part3.q: Why do many young people move from the countryside to cities?
part3.sample: The main reason is jobs. Cities offer far more opportunities, especially in industries like technology and finance, and salaries are usually much higher. Education is another factor. The best universities are in cities, and many graduates simply stay where they studied. There's also the lifestyle. Young people are attracted by entertainment and the feeling of being where things happen. Unfortunately, this leaves many villages with mainly elderly residents and children whose parents work far away.

part3.q: What are the advantages of living in the countryside compared with living in a city?
part3.sample: The most obvious advantages are cleaner air and a slower pace of life. People in rural areas tend to know their neighbours well, so there's a stronger sense of community. Housing is also much cheaper, which means families can have more space and less debt. On the other hand, services like hospitals and good schools can be hours away, which is a real problem for older people. So the countryside probably suits some stages of life better than others.

part3.q: Can tourism help to improve life in rural areas?
part3.sample: Yes, if it's managed well. Rural tourism brings money into villages through guesthouses, local food and handicrafts, and it can give young people a reason to return home and start a business. However, there are risks. If too many visitors arrive, villages can lose their character and turn into something like theme parks, with the same souvenir shops everywhere. The best approach is for local people to have a real say in how tourism develops, so that the benefits stay in the community.

part3.q: How do you think villages will change in the next few decades?
part3.sample: I expect many small, remote villages to keep shrinking as older residents pass away. At the same time, better internet and transport could make rural life more attractive to some people, particularly those who can work remotely. We might see certain villages turning into small hubs for tourism, organic farming or creative businesses. Agriculture will probably become more mechanised too, so fewer people will be needed to farm the same amount of land.

cueCard.title: Describe a building in your city that you find interesting.
cueCard.final: and explain why you find it interesting.

sample:
The building I'd like to describe is the old post office in the centre of my city. It's on a busy corner near the river, surrounded by modern office towers and shopping malls, which makes it stand out even more.

It was built in the 1920s, so it's almost a hundred years old. It's only three storeys high, made of red brick with white stone around the windows, and there's a clock tower on top that still keeps perfect time. Inside, the main hall has a high ceiling, a black-and-white tiled floor and long wooden counters that have been polished smooth by generations of customers' elbows. Walking in feels a bit like stepping into an old film.

Surprisingly, it's still a working post office, so people go there to send parcels and pay bills, just as they did a century ago. But a few years ago, part of the second floor was turned into a small postal museum, with old post boxes, uniforms and a huge stamp collection. There's also a cafe on the ground floor, where you can buy postcards and send them from a special post box that adds a commemorative postmark.

I find it interesting for a couple of reasons. As a child I collected stamps, so the museum feels like a grown-up version of my old albums. But more than that, I like the fact that the building hasn't been frozen in time. It still serves a practical purpose while keeping its history alive. Whenever I pass by and hear the clock strike, it reminds me that my city has a much longer story than its skyscrapers suggest.

part3.q: What makes a building beautiful?
part3.sample: Beauty is partly a matter of taste, of course, but certain things are widely appreciated. Good proportions matter, so that a building doesn't feel too heavy or out of balance. Natural materials like wood and stone also tend to age well, whereas cheap concrete often looks shabby after a few years. Above all, a beautiful building fits its surroundings. A glass tower might look stunning in a business district but completely out of place in a historic town.

part3.q: Why do many new buildings in cities look the same?
part3.sample: Mostly because of cost and speed. Developers want to build as many flats or offices as possible, as cheaply and quickly as possible, so they reuse the same designs again and again. Building regulations and standard materials also push designs in a similar direction. In China, cities expanded so rapidly over the last few decades that there simply wasn't time to think carefully about each building. As a result, many new districts look almost identical from one city to the next.

part3.q: Is it worth spending large amounts of public money on impressive public buildings?
part3.sample: Sometimes it is. A striking museum, library or concert hall can become a symbol of a city, attract tourists and give residents a sense of pride. However, there have been cases where local governments built enormous, expensive buildings that ended up half empty, while basic services were underfunded. So the key question is whether the building will actually be used by ordinary people. If it will, spending a bit more on good design is justified.

part3.q: Should local residents have a say in what new buildings look like?
part3.sample: They should, at least for large projects that change the character of a neighbourhood. Residents are the ones who live with the result every day, and they often know things that planners miss, such as how people actually use a street. That said, decisions can't be made by public vote alone, because people tend to resist anything new. A sensible system would involve public consultation, with final decisions made by experts who explain their reasoning openly.

cueCard.title: Describe a place you would like to visit in the future.
points: what you would like to do there
cueCard.final: and explain why you would like to visit this place.

sample:
The place I'd really like to visit is Dunhuang, a small city in Gansu Province, in the far north-west of China. It's on the edge of the desert, and it used to be an important stop on the ancient Silk Road, where traders and travellers passed between China and Central Asia.

I first heard about it at secondary school, when our history textbook had a photo of the Mogao Caves. These are hundreds of caves carved into a cliff, and inside them there are Buddhist wall paintings and statues, some of which are more than a thousand years old. More recently, I watched a short video series about the people who restore the paintings, and I was amazed by their patience. Some of them spend years working on a single wall.

If I go, the caves will definitely be my first stop. I've read that the number of visitors is limited each day to protect the paintings, so I'd need to book well in advance. I'd also like to visit the sand dunes just outside the city, where there's a small lake shaped like a crescent moon. I'm hoping to get up early, climb the dunes to watch the sunrise and then take some photos of the desert in the soft morning light.

The main reason I want to go is that it combines two things I love, history and photography. It's also completely different from where I live. My city is green, crowded and humid, so the idea of standing in a vast, silent desert is really appealing. I'm planning to go next autumn, when it's not too hot.

part3.q: Why do people want to travel to faraway places?
part3.sample: Partly it's curiosity. People want to see landscapes and cultures that are completely different from their everyday surroundings. There's also a feeling that the further you go, the bigger the adventure, and the better the stories you bring home. Social media plays a role too, since a photo from a remote desert gets far more attention than one from the local park. And for some people, travelling far is a way of escaping work pressure and really switching off.

part3.q: Should the number of tourists at famous historical sites be limited?
part3.sample: Yes, it's often necessary. At sites like ancient caves or old temples, the breath and humidity from thousands of visitors can actually damage paintings and structures. Overcrowding also spoils the experience, because it's hard to appreciate anything while you're being pushed along by a crowd. Limits can be unfair to people who can't plan far ahead, so a booking system that keeps some tickets for same-day visitors seems like a fair compromise. Protecting these places for future generations should come first.

part3.q: Will virtual reality ever replace real travel?
part3.sample: I doubt it will fully replace it, although it could become a useful alternative. Virtual tours are already impressive, and they allow people who are elderly, disabled or short of money to explore places they could never reach. They could also reduce pressure on fragile sites. But travel involves much more than seeing. It's the smell of the food, the conversations with strangers and even the things that go wrong. Technology can't reproduce all of that, at least not in the near future.

part3.q: What impact does international tourism have on the environment?
part3.sample: The impact is significant. Flying produces a large amount of carbon emissions, and long-haul flights are among the most polluting things an individual can do. Popular destinations also suffer from problems like plastic waste, water shortages and damage to coral reefs or wildlife habitats. On the other hand, tourism money can fund national parks and conservation projects. So the challenge is to travel less often but more responsibly, for example by staying longer in one place and choosing trains where possible.

cueCard.title: Describe a photograph you took that you are proud of.
points: when and where you took it
cueCard.final: and explain why you are proud of it.

sample:
The photo I'd like to talk about is a black-and-white picture of an old man repairing bicycles at a roadside stall. I took it about a year and a half ago, early on a Sunday morning, in a narrow lane in the old part of my city, not long after I'd bought my second-hand camera.

The stall wasn't much, just a wooden table, a pump and a few boxes of tools under a faded umbrella. The man was probably in his seventies, and when I first walked past, he was concentrating on fixing a puncture, with his glasses pushed up onto his forehead. The early light was coming in sideways between the buildings, lighting up his hands and the wheel he was holding.

I didn't want to take his picture without permission, so I asked him first. He laughed and said I could, as long as I didn't make him look too old. I took about twenty shots, moving around slowly so I wouldn't disturb him, and the one I chose shows his hands in sharp focus with his face slightly blurred behind them. Later, I converted it to black and white, because the colours were a bit distracting.

I'm proud of it for a few reasons. First, it was the first time I'd felt brave enough to photograph a stranger up close. Second, it captures something that's disappearing. Stalls like his used to be on every corner, but now most people ride shared bikes. When I went back a few months later, the stall had gone. I'd printed a copy for him, so I left it with his neighbour, and I still keep one above my desk.

part3.q: Why do people take so many photos nowadays?
part3.sample: The obvious answer is that it's become so easy. Everyone carries a decent camera in their pocket, and taking a picture costs nothing, unlike in the days of film, when every shot had to count. Social media has also changed why people take photos. It's no longer just about remembering a moment but about sharing it and getting a reaction. The result is that we take thousands of photos but rarely look at most of them again.

part3.q: Does taking photos help people remember things, or does it stop them from enjoying the moment?
part3.sample: It can do both. A photo is a great way to bring back memories you'd otherwise lose, and looking through old albums is one of my favourite things to do with my family. However, when people are busy filming a whole concert or photographing every dish at dinner, they're seeing the experience through a screen rather than living it. The trips I remember most vividly are actually the ones where I put my camera away for long periods.

part3.q: Should news photographs ever be edited?
part3.sample: Basic adjustments, like making a dark photo slightly brighter, are probably acceptable. But changing the content of a news photo, for example removing a person or adding smoke, is a different matter. News is supposed to be a record of what actually happened, and if people discover that photos have been manipulated, they stop trusting the media altogether. With AI tools making fake images easier than ever, news organisations need strict rules and should be open about any editing they do.

part3.q: Is photography a form of art?
part3.sample: Yes, I believe it can be. Some people argue that a camera simply records what's in front of it, whereas a painter creates something from nothing. But a good photographer makes many artistic decisions, like what to include in the frame, when to press the shutter and how to use light. Two people standing in the same spot can produce completely different pictures. Of course, not every holiday snap is art, just as not every drawing is.

cueCard.title: Describe a toy you liked when you were a child.
cueCard.final: and explain why you liked it.

sample:
When I was about seven, my favourite toy was a wind-up tin frog. It was bright green with yellow spots, about the size of my palm, and if you turned a little key on its side, it would hop across the floor making a clicking sound. Looking back, it was a pretty simple toy, but I adored it.

It was a present from my grandfather on my mum's side, the same person who later got me into stamp collecting. He bought it for me when I'd been stuck indoors for a week with a bad cold. I remember him pretending the frog had jumped out of his pocket by itself, and I was completely convinced for about five seconds.

I played with it in all sorts of ways. Sometimes I'd organise races between the frog and my toy cars, which the frog always lost because it kept hopping sideways. I also built obstacle courses for it out of books and slippers, and I'd make up stories about it crossing a dangerous swamp, which was usually the kitchen floor. When it broke after a year or so, my grandfather fixed the spring with a pair of pliers, though it never hopped quite as well again.

I think I liked it so much because it felt magical. There were no batteries or screens, so I had to use my imagination to bring it to life. It also reminds me of my grandfather, who passed away when I was at university. My mum found the frog in a drawer a few years ago, and it now sits on my bookshelf, slightly rusty but still in one piece.

part3.q: How have children's toys changed compared with the past?
part3.sample: The biggest change is technology. When I was young, toys were mostly simple objects like dolls, balls or building blocks, and many were homemade. Now a lot of toys have batteries, lights and sounds, and some connect to apps or even talk back to the child. Toys are also much cheaper and more plentiful, so many children have boxes full of them. In my opinion, that sometimes means each toy is valued less, and children get bored more quickly.

part3.q: Are electronic toys good for children?
part3.sample: Some can be useful, for example ones that teach basic coding or help children practise reading. However, I worry that many electronic toys do too much of the work. If a toy tells you exactly what to do and rewards you with flashing lights, there's not much room for imagination. Young children also need to move around and use their hands. So electronic toys are fine in moderation, but they shouldn't replace blocks, crayons and outdoor play.

part3.q: Should toys be designed differently for boys and girls?
part3.sample: I don't think they need to be. In many shops, you still see one aisle full of pink dolls and toy kitchens and another full of blue cars and toy guns, which sends children a message about what they're supposed to like. Plenty of girls enjoy building things, and plenty of boys like caring for dolls. Toys designed for all children allow them to explore different interests freely, and that could even influence the careers they choose later on.

part3.q: Should advertising aimed at children be restricted?
part3.sample: Yes, I believe it should. Young children can't easily tell the difference between an advert and a normal programme, so they're very easily influenced. Toy companies know this and use bright colours, cartoon characters and catchy songs to make children beg their parents for products. This puts financial pressure on families and encourages materialism from a young age. Some countries already restrict advertising during children's television, and similar rules should apply to online videos, where most kids now spend their time.

cueCard.title: Describe something you made by hand.
points: when and where you made it
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about making it.

sample:
I'd like to describe a small wooden stool that I made at a woodworking workshop last winter. It's about forty centimetres high, made of walnut, with a square seat and four slightly slanted legs. It's not perfect, but it's sturdy enough to stand on, and it now lives by the door of my flat, where I sit to put my shoes on.

The workshop is in a converted warehouse on the edge of the city, run by a carpenter who used to make furniture for hotels. I signed up for a weekend course with my flatmate, mainly because we both spend all week staring at screens and wanted to do something physical for a change. There were six of us in the class, and none of us had ever used proper tools before.

The whole process took two full days. First, the carpenter showed us how to measure and mark the wood, and then we cut the pieces with hand saws, which was much harder than it looked. The trickiest part was making the joints, because he insisted we use traditional techniques without a single nail. My first attempt was far too loose, so I had to start that piece all over again. On the second day, we sanded everything until it was smooth and finished it with oil, which brought out the colour of the wood beautifully.

I felt a mixture of frustration and satisfaction. There were moments when I wanted to give up, but finishing something real with my own hands felt incredibly rewarding, much more so than finishing a report at work. Every time I sit on it, I feel a small sense of pride.

part3.q: Why do fewer people make things by hand nowadays?
part3.sample: Mainly because it's cheaper and quicker to buy things. Factories can produce furniture, clothes and household items at prices that handmade goods can't compete with. People also have less free time than before, and learning a craft takes years of practice. In the past, skills like knitting or mending were passed down in families out of necessity. Now that we can replace almost anything with a few taps on a phone, there's much less reason to learn them.

part3.q: Are handmade products better than machine-made ones?
part3.sample: Not always. Machine-made products are often more consistent and precise, and they're affordable for most people, which is a big advantage. Handmade items, on the other hand, usually have more character, because each one is slightly different, and a skilled craftsperson may use better materials and pay more attention to detail. They also tend to last longer and can be repaired. So handmade is often better in quality, but it isn't realistic for everything we need.

part3.q: Should schools teach practical skills like cooking and woodwork?
part3.sample: I strongly believe they should. These skills are useful throughout life, and they give students who aren't strong academically a chance to shine. Making something with your hands also teaches patience and problem-solving in a very concrete way. In China, practical subjects used to be squeezed out by exam preparation, although I've read that schools are now required to offer more of this kind of education. That's a positive step, as long as it isn't treated as an afterthought.

part3.q: Will traditional crafts disappear in the future?
part3.sample: Some probably will, sadly, especially very specialised ones that few young people are willing to learn. However, I'm fairly optimistic about many others. There's growing interest in handmade goods among young city people, partly as a reaction against mass production and screen-based jobs. Online platforms also allow craftspeople to sell directly to customers all over the country. If governments support master craftspeople in training apprentices, many traditional skills can survive, even if they become more of a hobby than a trade.

cueCard.title: Describe a wedding you attended.
points: when and where it took place
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about this wedding.

sample:
I'd like to talk about the wedding of my university classmate Mei, which I went to last May. We'd shared a lot of late-night study sessions at university, so I was really happy when she sent me the invitation, which, like most invitations nowadays, arrived as a digital card on WeChat.

The wedding took place in her husband's hometown, a coastal city about four hours away by high-speed train. Rather than holding it in a big hotel banquet hall, which is still the most common choice, they had the ceremony outdoors on a lawn overlooking the sea. There were about eighty guests, and everything was decorated in white and pale blue, with lots of small lanterns hanging from the trees.

The day was a mix of old and new traditions. In the morning, there was the traditional door game, where the groom and his friends had to answer silly questions and hand out red envelopes before the bridesmaids would let him in to collect the bride. Later, during the ceremony, the couple served tea to both sets of parents, which was quite moving. But they also did some very modern things. Instead of long speeches from bosses or relatives, they showed a funny video about how they'd met through a hiking app, and dinner was a relaxed buffet rather than a twelve-course banquet.

Overall, I loved it because it felt so personal. It didn't feel like a show put on for the guests, and I could see that every detail reflected who they were. It also made me think about what I'd want for my own wedding one day, probably something small and relaxed like theirs.

part3.q: Why do some people spend a lot of money on weddings?
part3.sample: There are several reasons. In many cultures, a wedding is seen as one of the most important days of your life, so people want it to be perfect. In China, there's also the issue of face. Families may feel they need an impressive banquet to show their status to relatives and friends. Social media adds to the pressure, since couples see beautifully decorated weddings online and want something similar. Parents often contribute a lot of money too, and they may have their own expectations.

part3.q: How have weddings changed in your country in recent years?
part3.sample: They've become much more varied. A generation ago, almost every wedding followed the same pattern, a banquet at a restaurant with dozens of tables and a host telling jokes on stage. Now couples are choosing outdoor ceremonies, destination weddings or very small gatherings with only close family. Wedding photography has turned into a huge industry, with couples travelling to beaches or historic sites for photo shoots. At the same time, many customs, like the tea ceremony, are still kept, just in a more personal way.

part3.q: Why are people getting married later than they used to?
part3.sample: One reason is that people spend longer in education, so they start their careers later and want to feel financially secure before settling down. Housing is another big factor, since buying a flat in a big city is extremely expensive. Attitudes have also changed. Many young people, women in particular, are focused on their careers and personal development, and there's less social pressure to marry by a certain age. Some are also simply more cautious, having seen relatives go through difficult divorces.

part3.q: Will wedding traditions still be important in the future?
part3.sample: Some will survive, but they'll become more of a personal choice. Couples will probably keep the traditions that feel meaningful to them, like honouring their parents, and drop the ones that seem outdated or too expensive. Technology might also change things. More guests could join online, for example, if they live abroad. But as long as families care about marking important moments together, weddings are likely to keep a traditional core.

cueCard.title: Describe a concert or live performance you went to.
points: when and where it took place
cueCard.final: and explain why you enjoyed it.

sample:
The performance I'd like to describe is an outdoor music festival I went to last summer. It was held over a weekend on a big riverside lawn just outside my city, and there were around twenty bands, mostly indie and folk groups, playing on two stages from early afternoon until late at night.

I went with my flatmate and two friends from my badminton group. We'd bought tickets months in advance, as soon as the line-up was announced, because one of my favourite indie bands was headlining on the Saturday night. We took the metro to the last stop and then a shuttle bus, which was packed with people in festival T-shirts, so the excitement started even before we arrived.

The afternoon was quite relaxed. We spread out a picnic blanket near the smaller stage, ate street food and discovered a couple of bands we'd never heard of, including one that mixed traditional Chinese instruments with electric guitars, which sounded surprisingly good. Then, as the sun went down, everyone moved towards the main stage. When the headliners came on, the crowd went wild. They played almost all their best-known songs, and at one point the lead singer stopped and let the audience sing a whole chorus. Thousands of people singing the same words in the dark is something I'll never forget.

I enjoyed it so much because it was such a contrast to my usual routine. For one day, I wasn't thinking about emails or deadlines at all. I also loved the shared feeling with complete strangers. Everyone was there for the same reason, and the atmosphere was incredibly friendly.

part3.q: Why do people enjoy going to live performances?
part3.sample: Mainly for the atmosphere. When you're surrounded by thousands of people who love the same music, there's a shared energy that you just can't get from headphones. Live performances also feel unique, since no two shows are exactly the same, and something unexpected might happen. For many people, it's a social event as well, a chance to spend time with friends and create memories together. And seeing a famous performer in person makes them feel more real and less distant.

part3.q: Should governments provide funding for the arts, such as music and theatre?
part3.sample: Yes, at least to some extent. Commercial pop concerts can support themselves through ticket sales, but art forms like traditional opera, classical music or experimental theatre often can't survive without help. They're part of a country's cultural heritage, and once they disappear, they're very hard to revive. Funding can also make the arts accessible to people on low incomes, for example through cheap tickets for students. Of course, the money needs to be spent transparently and fairly.

part3.q: Why are concert tickets so expensive nowadays?
part3.sample: Partly because musicians now earn very little from recorded music. Streaming platforms pay tiny amounts per play, so touring has become the main source of income for many artists. Large concerts are also extremely costly to put on, with huge stages, lighting and security. On top of that, there's the problem of ticket touts, who buy up tickets in bulk and resell them at several times the original price. Some organisers now require tickets to be registered under real names, which seems to help.

part3.q: Will virtual concerts become more popular in the future?
part3.sample: They probably will, to some extent. During the pandemic, many artists performed online, and some of those shows attracted millions of viewers. As virtual reality improves, watching a concert from home could feel far more immersive, and it would cost much less than travelling to a stadium. However, they're unlikely to replace real concerts. Part of the appeal of live music is the physical experience, like feeling the bass in your chest and singing with the crowd. Virtual concerts will more likely be an extra option.

cueCard.title: Describe an event organised by your company or school that you took part in.
points: when and where it was held
what you did at the event
cueCard.final: and explain whether you enjoyed it.

sample:
The event I'd like to talk about is my company's annual dinner, which took place this January, a couple of weeks before the Spring Festival. Almost every Chinese company holds one of these at the end of the year. It's a mix of a party, an awards ceremony and a talent show, and it's a pretty big deal.

Ours was held in the ballroom of a hotel near the office, and about three hundred employees attended. Each department is expected to prepare a performance, and this year our marketing team somehow ended up doing a comedy sketch. Since I'd written most of the script, I couldn't really avoid being in it. We rehearsed in a meeting room after work for about three weeks, and I was nervous right up until the moment we walked on stage.

The evening followed the usual pattern. First, the CEO gave a speech about the company's achievements, and then there were awards for outstanding employees. After that came the performances, which ranged from a very professional dance by the sales team to a rather painful karaoke song by the finance director. Our sketch was about a client who keeps changing his mind, and because everyone in the room had experienced something similar, it got a lot of laughs. The night ended with a lucky draw, and I won a rice cooker, which I passed on to my parents.

Overall, I did enjoy it, more than I'd expected. The rehearsals took up a lot of my free time, which was a bit stressful, but performing together brought our team much closer. And seeing our serious senior managers dancing badly was definitely worth it.

part3.q: Why do companies organise social events for their employees?
part3.sample: The main goal is usually to build team spirit. When colleagues from different departments spend time together outside normal work, they get to know each other, which can make cooperation easier later. Events like annual dinners are also a way for companies to thank staff and recognise achievements, which can improve morale and loyalty. And from a practical point of view, a company with a lively culture finds it easier to attract and keep talented employees, especially younger ones.

part3.q: Should employees be required to take part in work events outside working hours?
part3.sample: I don't think they should be. People have families, hobbies and other responsibilities, and their evenings and weekends should belong to them. Forcing people to attend often creates resentment, which defeats the purpose of the event. In some Chinese companies, staff are expected to rehearse performances for weeks without extra pay, and that has become quite a controversial issue online. If an event is well organised and genuinely fun, most people will choose to come anyway.

part3.q: How has company culture in your country changed in recent years?
part3.sample: There have been some noticeable changes, especially in newer industries like technology. Offices have become more informal, with flatter structures, casual dress and open-plan spaces. Younger employees are also more willing to question long working hours. A few years ago, there was a big public debate about the culture of working from nine in the morning to nine at night, six days a week. On the other hand, traditional hierarchies are still strong in many state-owned companies and older businesses.

part3.q: Will people's working lives be very different in the future?
part3.sample: They're likely to be quite different. Automation and artificial intelligence will probably take over many routine tasks, so people will need to retrain several times during their careers. Remote and flexible working could become even more common, which would give people more control over their time but also make it harder to separate work from home life. We might also see shorter working weeks in some countries if productivity keeps rising. Either way, lifelong learning will be essential.

cueCard.title: Describe a time when someone gave you useful advice.
cueCard.final: and explain why the advice was useful.

sample:
I'd like to talk about some advice I got from my manager, Ms Wang, during my first few months at the company where I still work. It was about giving presentations, which back then was my biggest weakness.

As a junior member of the marketing team, I occasionally had to present campaign ideas to clients. I was terrified of these meetings, so I'd write out every single word of my presentation and try to memorise it. The result was a disaster. I spoke too fast, avoided eye contact, and if anyone interrupted with a question, I completely lost my place. After one particularly bad meeting, Ms Wang invited me for a coffee, and I was sure she was about to tell me off.

Instead, she gave me some really practical advice. She told me to throw away the script and focus on just three key messages that I wanted the client to remember. For each message, I should prepare one real example or story, because people remember stories far better than statistics. She also suggested that I practise by explaining my ideas to a friend who knew nothing about marketing. If they could understand it, the client would too.

That advice turned out to be incredibly useful. The next time I presented, I still felt nervous, but because I wasn't trying to recall a script, I could actually listen to the client and respond naturally. Over time, presentations became one of my strengths, and last year I even trained some new colleagues using the same approach. More generally, it taught me that preparation isn't about memorising more, but about understanding what really matters.

part3.q: Who do young people usually ask for advice?
part3.sample: It depends on the issue. For personal matters, like relationships, most young people turn to friends of the same age, because they feel friends understand them better than parents do. For bigger decisions, such as choosing a university or a job, parents and teachers still play an important role, at least in China. Increasingly, though, young people look for advice online, through forums, videos or social media influencers, which is convenient but not always reliable.

part3.q: Is advice from professionals more valuable than advice from family and friends?
part3.sample: In certain areas, definitely. If you have a health or legal problem, a doctor or a lawyer has expert knowledge that family members simply don't have. However, professionals don't know you as a person. Family and friends understand your personality, your history and what really matters to you, so their advice on personal choices can be more suitable. The ideal is probably to combine the two, getting the facts from experts and then talking the decision through with people who know you well.

part3.q: Why do some people find it hard to accept advice?
part3.sample: Pride is a big part of it. Accepting advice can feel like admitting that you've failed or that someone else knows better, which is uncomfortable, especially for people in senior positions. The way advice is given also matters. If it sounds like criticism or a lecture, people become defensive. And sometimes people have already decided what they want to do, so they only listen to advice that supports their decision. Young people in particular may prefer to learn from their own mistakes.

part3.q: Will people rely more on artificial intelligence for advice in the future?
part3.sample: I think they will, and to some extent they already do. AI assistants are available at any time, they never get tired of questions, and they can draw on huge amounts of information, so they're useful for practical problems like planning a budget or understanding a medical term. But there are risks. AI can make confident mistakes, and it doesn't truly understand people's feelings or circumstances. For emotional or life-changing decisions, most people will probably still want advice from someone they trust.

cueCard.title: Describe a time when you lost something important.
points: when and where you lost it
what you did to find it
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about the experience.

sample:
I'd like to talk about the evening I lost my phone in a taxi, which happened about a year ago. I'd been at a team dinner that finished quite late, so I took a taxi home instead of the metro. I was so tired that I must have put my phone down on the seat while I was looking for my keys.

I only realised it was gone when I got to my front door and reached into my pocket. For a moment, I just stood there in a panic. In China, your phone is basically your wallet, your ID and your diary all in one, so without it, I couldn't pay for anything or even contact anyone. Luckily, my flatmate was home, so I borrowed their phone and called my own number, but it was switched off. Then I remembered that I'd hailed the taxi on the street rather than through an app, so there was no online record of the driver. Fortunately, I'd kept the paper receipt, which had the taxi company's number on it. I rang them, explained what had happened, and they promised to contact the driver.

The next morning, the driver called my flatmate's number and said he'd found my phone under the back seat. He even drove over to my building before starting his shift. I tried to give him some money to thank him, but he refused, so I sent a thank-you letter to his company instead.

Looking back, I felt terrible that night, mainly because I realised how dependent I'd become on one small device. But in the end, I was touched by the driver's honesty.

part3.q: Why do people often lose things nowadays?
part3.sample: The main reason is probably that people are constantly distracted. We're often looking at our phones or thinking about several things at once, so we don't notice where we put things down. Modern life is also very fast. People rush between work, the gym and social events, carrying lots of small items like earphones, keys and power banks. Stress and lack of sleep make the problem worse, since they affect our memory and concentration.

part3.q: Are people more willing to return lost property now than in the past?
part3.sample: It's hard to say whether people are more honest, but returning things has definitely become easier. In China, public transport and taxi companies have well-organised lost property systems, and security cameras are almost everywhere, which may encourage people to hand things in. With mobile payments, very few people carry cash, so a lost wallet often contains little that's useful to a stranger. In smaller communities in the past, neighbours knew each other, so returning things was also a matter of reputation.

part3.q: Should people who return lost items receive a reward?
part3.sample: A reward is a nice gesture, but it shouldn't be compulsory. If someone returns something valuable, offering them a small sum of money or a gift is a good way to show appreciation, and it might encourage others to do the same. However, if rewards were expected, people might start returning things only for the money, which would change the nature of the act. Honesty should be its own reward, but gratitude is always welcome.

part3.q: Has technology made it easier to find lost items?
part3.sample: Yes, in many ways. Phones can be tracked with GPS, and you can buy small tracking devices to attach to keys or bags. Ride-hailing apps keep a record of every trip, so contacting a driver takes seconds. Social media also helps, since people post photos of lost pets or items in neighbourhood groups, and these often get shared widely. The flip side is that we now carry more valuable devices than ever, so losing one is a much bigger problem than losing a set of keys used to be.

cueCard.title: Describe a film that made a strong impression on you.
cueCard.final: and explain why it made a strong impression on you.

sample:
The film I'd like to talk about is Coco, an animated film made by Pixar. I first watched it at the cinema when it came out, but I watched it again last spring with my flatmate, and it made an even stronger impression on me the second time.

The story is set in Mexico and centres on a twelve-year-old boy called Miguel, who dreams of becoming a musician. The problem is that his family has banned music for generations, because his great-great-grandfather supposedly abandoned the family to pursue a music career. On the Day of the Dead, a festival when Mexican families remember relatives who have died, Miguel accidentally crosses into the Land of the Dead. There he meets his ancestors and a charming but scruffy skeleton called Hector, and he has to find a way home before sunrise. Without giving too much away, there's a big twist, and it turns out that the family history he'd been told wasn't quite true.

The reason it made such an impression on me is its central idea, that people only truly die when no one remembers them any more. That really struck a chord, because it's similar to the Chinese tradition of Qingming, when we visit our ancestors' graves and tell stories about them. I watched it a few weeks after the anniversary of my grandfather's death, and I ended up in tears during the final song, which Miguel sings to his very old great-grandmother.

Afterwards, I phoned my grandmother and asked her to tell me more about my grandfather's childhood, which is something I'd never done before.

part3.q: Why are animated films popular with adults as well as children?
part3.sample: Many animated films are deliberately made to work on two levels. Children enjoy the colourful characters and humour, while adults pick up on deeper themes, such as loss, identity or family conflict, as well as jokes that go over children's heads. Animation also allows filmmakers to create worlds that would be impossible or too expensive with real actors. And for many adults, watching animation brings back a sense of childhood, which can be a welcome escape from everyday stress.

part3.q: Do films help people understand other cultures?
part3.sample: They can, to a certain extent. Before watching Coco, I knew almost nothing about Mexican traditions, and it made me curious enough to read more. Films let you see how people in other countries live, celebrate and relate to each other. However, they can also create stereotypes, especially when a culture is portrayed by outsiders who exaggerate certain features for entertainment. So films are a good starting point, but they shouldn't be the only way we learn about other places.

part3.q: Should foreign films be dubbed or shown with subtitles?
part3.sample: Personally, I prefer subtitles, because you hear the actors' real voices and emotions, and it's also a good way to pick up a foreign language. However, dubbing has its advantages. Young children and older people who read slowly may find subtitles hard to follow, and with dubbing you can focus completely on the images. The ideal situation is for cinemas and streaming platforms to offer both versions, so that viewers can choose whatever suits them.

part3.q: Will people still go to the cinema in the future?
part3.sample: I believe they will, but probably less often, and for different reasons. Streaming services have made it so easy to watch new films at home that people are choosier about what they see in cinemas. Big, spectacular films with amazing visual effects will still draw crowds, because they're simply better on a huge screen. Cinemas may also need to offer more of an experience, like comfortable seats, good food or special events, to compete with the sofa at home.

cueCard.title: Describe a podcast or radio programme you like listening to.
points: how you found out about it
when and where you listen to it
cueCard.final: and explain why you like listening to it.

sample:
I'd like to talk about a Chinese podcast about the history of everyday objects. Its name roughly translates as Small Things, Long Stories. Each episode lasts around forty minutes and takes one ordinary object, such as chopsticks, umbrellas or even instant noodles, and explains where it came from and how it changed people's lives.

I found out about it about a year ago through a colleague. We were chatting over lunch about why takeaway boxes are shaped the way they are, and she said I had to listen to an episode about food packaging. I listened to it on the way home that evening and ended up binge-listening to five more episodes over the weekend.

These days I listen to it mainly on my commute. My metro journey takes nearly an hour, and a new episode comes out every Tuesday, so it's become a regular part of my week. I also listen while I'm doing housework, like washing up or tidying my room, because it makes boring jobs much more bearable.

There are several reasons I like it. Firstly, the two hosts, a historian and a former journalist, have great chemistry. They tease each other a lot, but they're clearly passionate about the subject. Secondly, I learn something surprising in almost every episode. For instance, I had no idea that instant noodles were invented in Japan in 1958, or that they were originally more expensive than fresh noodles. Lastly, it changes the way I see my surroundings. After an episode about bricks, I spent a whole weekend photographing old brick walls around the city, which my friends found hilarious. It makes ordinary life feel a little more interesting.

part3.q: Why have podcasts become so popular in recent years?
part3.sample: One big reason is convenience. You can listen while commuting, exercising or cooking, so podcasts fit into time that would otherwise be wasted. Unlike videos, they don't require you to look at a screen. The range of topics is also enormous, from true crime to economics, so almost everyone can find something that matches their interests. And many people enjoy the informal, conversational style. Listening to the same hosts every week can feel like spending time with friends.

part3.q: Is listening a better way to learn than reading?
part3.sample: It depends on the person and the content. Listening works well for stories and discussions, and it's accessible to people who struggle with reading or have poor eyesight. However, reading usually allows a deeper understanding of complex material, because you can go at your own pace, reread difficult parts and take notes. When I listen to podcasts, I often realise later that I've missed something important because my mind wandered. So for serious study, reading still has the edge.

part3.q: Do people trust traditional media, such as newspapers and radio, less than they used to?
part3.sample: In many countries, trust does seem to have declined. People now get news from many different sources, and they're more aware that traditional media can be influenced by owners, advertisers or governments. At the same time, a lot of misinformation spreads on social media, so some people actually turn back to established newspapers when they want reliable facts. In my experience, older people tend to trust traditional outlets more, while younger people rely on online creators they feel connected to.

part3.q: How do you think people will get their news in the future?
part3.sample: I expect news to become even more personalised. AI systems will probably select and summarise stories based on each person's interests, perhaps delivering a short audio briefing every morning. That's convenient, but it risks trapping people in bubbles where they only hear opinions they already agree with. Short videos will also remain a major source of news for young people. Hopefully, there will still be demand for in-depth reporting, even if people have to pay for it through subscriptions.
